chunks.title: Corneal layers & numbers
chunks.tldr: 5 layers: epithelium, Bowman, stroma (90%), Descemet, endothelium. Endothelium can't regenerate: ~3000 cells/mm² young; oedema below ~500.
points: Cornea gives ~¾ of the eye's focusing power. No blood vessels. Most densely innervated tissue in the body (V1) → abrasions hurt a lot.
Size: 11.5 mm vertical × 12 mm horizontal. Centre ~540 µm thick, thicker at the edge.
Epithelium: basal cells → wing cells → surface cells. Stem cells at the limbus (palisades of Vogt). Loss → conjunctivalisation.
Bowman layer: acellular collagen. Doesn't regenerate.
Stroma: 90%. Regular collagen spacing = clarity. Scars but can't regenerate.
Descemet: basement membrane of the endothelium. Front part made before birth, back part grows lifelong. Can regenerate.
Endothelium: one layer of hexagonal cells that pump water out. Lose ~0.6%/year. <500 cells/mm² → oedema.
Proposed 6th layer: Dua layer (pre-Descemet).
chunks.hook: Endothelium = the cornea's bilge pump. No spare parts.
pearls: Before cataract surgery: oedema is likely below ~700 cells/mm², unlikely above 1000.

cards.q: Approximate endothelial cell count at which corneal oedema develops?
Which corneal layer can regenerate: Bowman or Descemet?

chunks.title: Superficial corneal signs
chunks.tldr: Where the punctate staining sits tells you the cause: top = VKC/SLK/floppy lid, middle band = dry eye/exposure, bottom = blepharitis/lagophthalmos/drops.
points: PEE (punctate epithelial erosions): tiny defects that stain with fluorescein.
Superior: VKC, chlamydia, SLK, floppy eyelid, contact lens trauma.
Interpalpebral: dry eye, reduced sensation, UV burn.
Inferior: blepharitis, lagophthalmos, drop toxicity, self-inflicted, trichiasis, entropion.
Central: overwearing contact lenses.
PEK (punctate epithelial keratitis): swollen grey epithelial cells. Viral (adeno, HSV, VZV, molluscum), chlamydia, Thygeson, drops.
Subepithelial infiltrates: adenovirus, zoster, chlamydia, marginal keratitis, rosacea, Thygeson.
Filaments: dry eye (mostly), SLK, neurotrophic, patching.
Epithelial oedema → microcysts → bullae: endothelial failure or sudden high IOP.
Pannus = superficial vessels + degenerative tissue under the epithelium.
chunks.hook: Top = allergy/SLK. Middle = dry. Bottom = lids & drops.

cards.q: Inferior punctate staining in a glaucoma patient on 3 drops?
Most common cause of corneal filaments?

chunks.title: Deep signs: infective or sterile? (PEDAL)
chunks.tldr: PEDAL: Pain, Epithelial defect, Discharge, AC reaction, Location. Big, central, painful, defect, pus, cells → infective.
points: Infective infiltrate: bigger, fast, large epithelial defect, more pain, purulent discharge, single, one eye, strong AC reaction, often central.
Sterile infiltrate: small, slow, little/no defect, mild pain, often multiple, both eyes, peripheral.
Ulcer = excavation + epithelial defect. Melt = enzyme breakdown with little infiltrate (e.g. PUK).
Ghost vessels: old unperfused deep vessels (see with retroillumination). Lipid leaks from vessels.
Descemet folds (striate keratopathy): oedema, inflammation, surgery, hypotony.
Descemetocoele: Descemet bulging into a deep ulcer: about to perforate.
Descemet breaks: Haab striae (congenital glaucoma, horizontal), keratoconus (→ hydrops), forceps birth injury (vertical).
Seidel test: fluorescein turns bright green where aqueous leaks.
chunks.hook: PEDAL hard to decide: infection or sterile?

cards.q: What does a positive Seidel test show?
cards.a: Aqueous leaking through the cornea (dilution of fluorescein to bright green).

cards.q: Bubble of Descemet membrane in the base of a deep ulcer?

chunks.title: Corneal drawings, imaging & healing tricks
chunks.tldr: Healing rule: a cornea rarely thins if the epithelium is intact. Tools: lubricants, bandage CL, lid closure, amniotic membrane, glue, stem cell grafts.
points: Drawing colours: scar = black, oedema = blue, hypopyon = yellow, vessels = red (wavy = superficial, straight = deep), pigment = brown.
Specular microscopy: endothelial cell count and shape (normal = regular hexagons). For pre-op risk, donor corneas, guttata, PPMD.
Topography (Placido) / Scheimpflug: keratoconus screening before refractive surgery.
Steroids: careful. They help HSV and fungi grow and slow healing.
Promote healing: stop toxic/preserved drops, lubricate, bandage CL (pain relief, protection, seals a tiny leak).
Lid closure: botox ptosis (2–3 months), tarsorrhaphy.
Gundersen conjunctival flap: for a chronic ulcer with poor visual prognosis.
Amniotic membrane: persistent epithelial defects. Cyanoacrylate glue + bandage lens: small perforations.
Limbal stem cell transplant (auto from the other eye, or allo): chemical burns, cicatrising disease.
Stop smoking: slows epithelial healing.
chunks.hook: Keep the skin on (epithelium) and the cornea won't melt.

cards.q: Treatment option for a small corneal perforation?
cards.a: Cyanoacrylate tissue glue + bandage contact lens.

cards.q: In corneal diagrams, how are deep vessels drawn?
cards.a: Straight red lines starting at the limbus.

chunks.title: Bacterial keratitis: who & what
chunks.tldr: Biggest risk = contact lenses (soft > rigid). Pseudomonas causes >60% of CL ulcers and melts fast.
points: Most bacteria need a damaged epithelium. Ones that get through healthy epithelium: N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, C. diphtheriae, H. influenzae.
Pseudomonas: Gram-negative rod, aggressive, >60% of CL keratitis, can perforate.
Staph aureus: well-defined white/yellow infiltrate. Strep: often aggressive.

Risks: contact lenses (esp. extended, soft, poor hygiene; even daily disposables), trauma, LASIK (atypical mycobacteria), ocular surface disease (HSV, bullous keratopathy, dry eye, exposure, trichiasis), immunosuppression, diabetes, vitamin A deficiency.
Symptoms: pain, photophobia, blur, discharge.
Signs: epithelial defect + bigger infiltrate, injection, stromal oedema, hypopyon, plaque KPs, can → descemetocoele → perforation.
Getting better = less lid swelling, smaller defect, less dense infiltrate, quieter AC.
Reduced corneal sensation → think neurotrophic, HSV.
chunks.hook: Contact lens + painful red eye = ulcer until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Most common organism in contact lens–related bacterial keratitis?
Name 2 bacteria that can penetrate intact corneal epithelium.
cards.a: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis (also C. diphtheriae, H. influenzae).

chunks.title: Scraping & lab: which plate for which bug
chunks.tldr: Scrape the edge and base. Plates: blood (most bacteria), chocolate (Neisseria, Haemophilus, Moraxella), Sabouraud (fungi), E. coli on non-nutrient agar (Acanthamoeba).
points: Use preservative-free anaesthetic (proxymetacaine). Clear mucus/debris first.
Scrape with a blade, needle or Kimura spatula. Smear on slides for Gram stain, then plate without breaking the agar.
Or: one scrape into brain–heart infusion broth.
Also culture: contact lens case, solutions, lenses (don't let the patient clean the case!).
Gram stain: purple = Gram-positive, pink = Gram-negative.
Other stains: Giemsa (bacteria, fungi, Acanthamoeba), calcofluor white (Acanthamoeba, fungi), Ziehl–Neelsen (mycobacteria, Nocardia), PAS, Grocott silver.
Special media: Löwenstein–Jensen (mycobacteria, Nocardia), cooked meat broth (anaerobes like P. acnes).
Already on antibiotics? Can stop for 12 h before scraping.
chunks.hook: Chocolate for the fussy ones (Neisseria, Haemophilus). E. coli is Acanthamoeba's lunch.

cards.q: Culture medium for Acanthamoeba?
cards.a: Non-nutrient agar seeded with E. coli.

cards.q: Stain for mycobacteria and Nocardia?

chunks.title: Treating bacterial keratitis
chunks.tldr: Hourly broad-spectrum drops day and night for 24–48 h: fluoroquinolone alone, or fortified cefuroxime + gentamicin. Steroids only after it's improving (SCUT).
points: Stop contact lenses. Shield if thin. Admit if poor compliance, severe, or only eye.
Monotherapy: fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin best penetration). Less toxic. Weaker on some Strep.
Ciprofloxacin can leave white corneal precipitates.
Duotherapy (aggressive or Strep): fortified cefuroxime 5% + gentamicin 1.5%. Expensive, short shelf-life, toxic.
Tailor: Gram+ cocci → cefuroxime/vancomycin. Gram− rods → gentamicin/FQ/ceftazidime. Mycobacteria → amikacin/clarithromycin. Nocardia → amikacin/co-trimoxazole.
Cycloplegic for pain and synechiae.
Steroids: start after 24–48 h of improvement. Never if fungus or mycobacteria suspected. SCUT: helped only severe/central cases.
Systemic: Neisseria/H. flu, perforation risk (ciprofloxacin + doxycycline for anti-collagenase), scleritis.
Not improving at 48 h? Review lab, don't change if it's working. Still not better → stop 24 h, re-scrape, think fungus/Acanthamoeba, biopsy.
Toxicity from fortified drops can look like ongoing infection!
Perforation: bandage CL → glue → graft. Later: keratoplasty, RGP lens (after 3 months), cataract surgery.
chunks.hook: Hourly, broad, then narrow. Steroids = dessert, only once the main course works.

cards.q: Standard fortified duotherapy?
Why add oral doxycycline for a thinning ulcer?
When are steroids absolutely avoided in keratitis?

chunks.title: Fungal keratitis
chunks.tldr: Plant/vegetable trauma or long-term steroids. Fluffy, feathery edges, satellite lesions, can have an intact epithelium. Treat with natamycin (filamentous) or amphotericin (Candida).
points: Yeasts (Candida): temperate climates, sick ocular surface, steroids, grafts. Dense yellow-white infiltrate.
Filamentous (Fusarium, Aspergillus): tropics, plant/agricultural injury. Grey, fluffy margins, satellites, feathery branches, ring infiltrate.
Epithelium may be intact. Can go through intact Descemet → endophthalmitis.
Slower onset than bacteria, but can perforate.
Tests: KOH prep (fast), calcofluor white, Gram/Giemsa (~50%), Sabouraud, PCR (up to 90%). Fungi grow deep → biopsy if not better in 3–4 days. Confocal microscopy.
Treat: debride epithelium, hourly topical: Candida → amphotericin 0.15% or econazole. Filamentous → natamycin 5% or econazole. Voriconazole is an alternative.
Oral voriconazole/itraconazole/fluconazole if severe/limbal/endophthalmitis. Doxycycline for thinning. No steroids.
Keratoplasty if failing. Improvement is slow.
Microsporidia: HIV → diffuse PEK. Fumagillin + albendazole.
chunks.hook: Farmer + twig + fluffy ulcer = fungus. Natamycin for Non-yeast (filaments).

cards.q: First-line topical for filamentous fungal keratitis?
First-line topical for Candida keratitis?
Rapid stain for fungi from a corneal scrape?

chunks.title: HSV basics: latency & recurrence
chunks.tldr: HSV = commonest infectious cause of corneal blindness in rich countries. Hides in the trigeminal ganglion. Recurrence ~50% at 10 years.
points: HSV-1 = above the waist (face, eyes). HSV-2 = genital (rarely eyes, e.g. at birth).
Primary infection: childhood, droplets. Usually mild (fever, URTI) ± blepharitis, follicular conjunctivitis. Antivirals don't prevent later recurrences.
Latent virus in the trigeminal ganglion → can't be cured.
Triggers: fever, hormones, UV, trauma, trigeminal injury.
Recurrence: ~10% at 1 year, ~50% at 10 years. More attacks → more risk.
Severe disease risks: atopy, kids, immunosuppression, malnutrition, measles, malaria, topical steroids (→ geographic ulcer).
chunks.hook: HSV = a squatter in the trigeminal ganglion. You can't evict it, only keep it quiet.

cards.q: Where does HSV establish latency for ocular disease?
Approximate 10-year ocular recurrence rate after one episode?

chunks.title: HSV epithelial keratitis: the dendrite
chunks.tldr: Dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs: bed stains with fluorescein, edges with rose Bengal. Reduced corneal sensation. Steroids → geographic ulcer.
points: This is live virus replicating in the epithelium.
Swollen epithelial cells (stellate) → branching dendrite with end-bulbs.
Fluorescein stains the ulcer bed. Rose Bengal stains the virus-laden cells at the edges.
Corneal sensation reduced.
Inappropriate steroids → big geographic ('amoeboid') ulcer.
Also: subepithelial haze, mild AC activity, follicular conjunctivitis, lid vesicles, raised IOP (check the other eye first, disposable prism).
After healing: irregular epithelium, whorl pattern from long-term antivirals. Don't mistake it for active disease.
Scars build up with each recurrence. Can recur in a graft.
Tests rarely needed: PCR, culture. Giemsa → multinucleated giant cells.
chunks.hook: Dendrite = a tree with bulbs on the branch tips. Zoster's pseudodendrites have no bulbs.

cards.q: Which stain highlights the margins of a dendritic ulcer?
What converts a dendritic ulcer to a geographic ulcer?

chunks.title: Treating HSV epithelial keratitis
chunks.tldr: Topical aciclovir 3% ointment or ganciclovir gel 5×/day (99% heal in 2 weeks). No steroids for epithelial disease. Avoid prostaglandins for IOP.
points: Dendrite differentials: zoster pseudodendrite, healing abrasion, Acanthamoeba, graft rejection line, tyrosinaemia type 2, soft CL, drop toxicity (incl. Polyquad).
Topical: aciclovir 3% or ganciclovir 0.15% 5×/day. Trifluridine (needs 9×/day). Safe even for 60 days.
Debride 2 mm beyond the edge for resistant cases (+ antiviral).
Toxicity signs: PEEs, whorled epithelium, follicles, punctal stenosis. No whorl + not healing → not using the drops?
Oral aciclovir 400 mg 5×/day (or valaciclovir/famciclovir): kids, immunocompromised, bad surface, can't use drops.
Raised IOP: avoid prostaglandin drops (can reactivate herpes).
Won't heal: resistant strain → switch agent, combine, or it might be VZV.
chunks.hook: Epithelial = virus → antivirals only. Steroids here can melt the cornea.

cards.q: Topical treatment of a dendritic ulcer?
cards.a: Aciclovir 3% ointment or ganciclovir 0.15% gel 5× daily.

cards.q: Which glaucoma drop class should be avoided in herpetic eye disease?

chunks.title: Disciform & necrotizing stromal HSV
chunks.tldr: Disciform = round patch of stromal oedema + KPs underneath + Wessely ring. Immune → steroid + antiviral cover, taper over ≥4 weeks.
points: Disciform (endotheliitis): gradual blur, haloes, mild pain. May have no history of dendrites.
Signs: central disc of stromal (± epithelial) oedema, granulomatous KPs underneath, Descemet folds, Wessely ring (antigen-antibody), raised IOP, reduced sensation.
Repeated attacks → scarring and vessels. A cause of interstitial keratitis.
Treat: pred 1% QID + topical antiviral QID, reduce both together over ≥4 weeks. Stop the antiviral when down to pred 0.5% once daily. Some need long-term weak steroid.
Active dendrite at the same time → more antiviral, less steroid.
Ciclosporin can help taper steroids (e.g. steroid IOP rise).
Necrotizing stromal keratitis: live virus in the stroma → necrosis, melting, dense infiltrate, KPs. Treat like severe disciform + high-dose oral antiviral. Restore the epithelium.
Neurotrophic: non-healing defect with grey stroma (anaesthesia + drug toxicity). Minimise steroids.
chunks.hook: Disciform = immune → steroid (with antiviral umbrella).

cards.q: Ring of stromal haze around disciform keratitis?
Treatment of HSV disciform keratitis?
cards.a: Topical steroid with topical antiviral cover, tapered together over at least 4 weeks.

chunks.title: HSV iritis, prophylaxis & grafts
chunks.tldr: Long-term oral aciclovir 400 mg BD halves recurrences. Use it for grafts in HSV eyes. HSV iritis: high IOP + patchy iris atrophy.
points: Herpetic iridocyclitis: may have no active keratitis. Raised IOP (trabeculitis), patchy iris atrophy (see on transillumination). Aqueous PCR. Topical steroid ± oral aciclovir.
Prophylaxis: oral aciclovir 400 mg BD cuts epithelial and stromal recurrences by ~50%. Valaciclovir 500 mg daily is an alternative. Effect stops when you stop. Check kidney function.
For frequent, bilateral, only-eye disease.
Complications: secondary infection, glaucoma (missed), cataract, iris atrophy.
Keratoplasty in HSV eyes: high recurrence and rejection → oral aciclovir prophylaxis. Try a rigid CL first.
chunks.hook: HSV prevention: 400 twice a day keeps the herpes away.

cards.q: Prophylactic oral aciclovir dose for recurrent HSV keratitis?
Anterior uveitis with high IOP and patchy iris transillumination defects?

chunks.title: HZO: shingles of V1
chunks.tldr: Hutchinson sign (tip/side of nose) → high risk of eye involvement. Oral antiviral within 72 h (aciclovir 800 mg 5×/day, or valaciclovir 1 g TDS).
points: VZV = chickenpox + shingles. Lies dormant in sensory ganglia. Reactivates when immunity fades. 1 in 3 people get shingles.
Hutchinson sign: vesicles in the nasociliary area (tip/side of nose) → eye involvement likely.
Elderly → worse. HIV → severe; young patient with shingles → consider immunodeficiency.
Prodrome 3–5 days (tired, fever, burning pain) → red rash → vesicles (within 24 h) → pustules → crusts (2–3 weeks) → depigmented scars.
Rash respects the midline. Lid swelling can spread to the other side.
Zoster sine herpete = shingles with no rash.
Treat: oral aciclovir 800 mg 5×/day 7–10 days, or valaciclovir 1 g TDS / famciclovir. Within 72 h (later is OK if still vesicular). Cuts late eye complications by ~50%.
IV aciclovir: encephalitis, immunocompromised. Oral steroids help acute pain but not post-herpetic neuralgia.
Brivudine + 5-FU = fatal.
Contagious (chickenpox) until crusted. Vaccines for >50 years (live or recombinant).
chunks.hook: Nose tip = eye trip (Hutchinson sign).

cards.q: What is the Hutchinson sign?
cards.a: Vesicles on the tip/side of the nose (nasociliary nerve) → predicts ocular involvement in HZO.

cards.q: Ideal window to start oral antivirals in HZO?

chunks.title: HZO eye problems: early & late
chunks.tldr: Zoster pseudodendrites have no end-bulbs. Day 10 → nummular keratitis. Week 3 → stromal keratitis. Months → neurotrophic, mucous plaques. Iritis with sectoral iris atrophy.
points: Acute epithelial keratitis (>50%, day 2): small fine dendrites with tapered ends, no bulbs, stain better with rose Bengal.
Conjunctivitis, episcleritis (early). Scleritis (end of week 1) → oral NSAID/steroid.
Nummular keratitis (~day 10): granular subepithelial spots with a halo → steroids (recur if stopped early).
Stromal keratitis (~5%, week 3) → steroids, slow taper. Disciform less common than with HSV.
Anterior uveitis (≥1/3): sectoral iris atrophy, high IOP. Avoid prostaglandins.
Back of the eye: ARN, PORN (immunocompromised), retinal vasculitis. Always look!
Nerves: III palsy (commonest), IV, VI → usually recover in 6 months. Optic neuritis, encephalitis rare.
Chronic: neurotrophic keratopathy (up to 50%), scleral atrophy, mucous plaque keratitis (~5%, months 3–6 → steroid + acetylcysteine), lipid degeneration, lid scarring.
Can relapse years later; old lid scars are the clue.
chunks.hook: HZO timeline: Dendrite (day 2) → Nummular (day 10) → Stromal (week 3) → Plaques (months).

cards.q: How do HZO pseudodendrites differ from HSV dendrites?
cards.a: Finer, tapered ends without terminal bulbs; stain better with rose Bengal.

cards.q: Most common cranial nerve palsy in HZO?

chunks.title: Post-herpetic neuralgia
chunks.tldr: Pain >1 month after the rash heals. Up to 75% of over-70s. Treat with tricyclics, gabapentin, capsaicin/lidocaine patches. Watch for depression.
points: Constant or stabbing, worse at night, light touch hurts (allodynia).
Slowly improves: only ~2% still have it at 5 years.
Can cause severe depression and suicide risk → pain clinic.
Local: cold compress, capsaicin 0.075%, lidocaine 5% patch.
Systemic ladder: paracetamol → codeine → amitriptyline/nortriptyline → carbamazepine (stabbing pain) → gabapentin ± oxycodone.
chunks.hook: PHN: Pain Hangs oN past a month.

cards.q: Definition of post-herpetic neuralgia?
cards.a: Pain persisting more than 1 month after the rash has healed.

chunks.title: Interstitial keratitis: syphilis & Cogan
chunks.tldr: IK = stromal inflammation, epithelium spared. Late: ghost vessels + feathery deep scars. Always test for syphilis. Cogan = IK + deafness/vertigo.
points: Causes: syphilis (classic), HSV, VZV, TB, Lyme, parasites, sarcoid, Cogan.
Congenital syphilis: saddle nose, sabre tibiae, Hutchinson teeth, deafness, Clutton joints, rhagades. Eye: IK, uveitis, salt-and-pepper retinopathy, Argyll Robertson pupils.
Syphilitic IK: age 5–25, 80% both eyes. Severe blur, deep vessels + clouding = 'salmon patch', granulomatous uveitis.
Later: clears, vessels empty → ghost vessels, feathery deep scars.
Treat: topical steroid + cycloplegic + systemic penicillin (GUM/ID).
Cogan syndrome: young adults, autoimmune vasculitis. IK (peripheral, then central) + deafness, tinnitus, vertigo. Can have systemic vasculitis.
Cogan: urgent systemic steroids for hearing. Differential: Susac syndrome.
chunks.hook: Ghost vessels → think syphilis. Cogan = Cornea + Cochlea.

cards.q: Salmon patch in the cornea?
cards.a: Active syphilitic IK: deep stromal vessels obscured by clouding.

cards.q: Interstitial keratitis + sensorineural deafness + vertigo in a young adult?

chunks.title: Acanthamoeba keratitis
chunks.tldr: Contact lens + tap water. Pain way worse than it looks. Early radial keratoneuritis, later ring abscess. Treat with PHMB / chlorhexidine ± propamidine.
points: Free-living protozoa in soil and water. Cysts are tough. CL rinsed or stored in tap water, swimming in lenses.
Often misdiagnosed as HSV (pseudodendrites) or fungus.
Pain out of proportion to the signs.
Early: irregular grey epithelium, pseudodendrites, radial perineural infiltrates (nearly pathognomonic).
Later: ring infiltrate/abscess, scleritis (reactive), melt.
Lab: calcofluor white, PAS. Culture on non-nutrient agar + E. coli. PCR, confocal microscopy, biopsy.
Treat early: debride + PHMB 0.02% and/or chlorhexidine 0.02% (kill cysts) + hexamidine/propamidine (Brolene). Hourly, for months. Relapses common.
Steroids: avoid (maybe low dose after ≥2 weeks of treatment). Oral NSAID for pain. Keratoplasty if failing.
chunks.hook: Acanth-ouch-moeba: huge pain, small signs. Nerves light up (radial keratoneuritis).

cards.q: Virtually pathognomonic early sign of Acanthamoeba keratitis?
Which agents are cysticidal?

chunks.title: Marginal keratitis & phlyctenulosis
chunks.tldr: Marginal keratitis = sterile infiltrate with a clear gap from the limbus (staph hypersensitivity). Phlycten = white limbal nodule (staph, or TB in endemic areas).
points: Marginal keratitis: immune reaction to Staph antigens (immune complexes). Lids have blepharitis.
Signs: subepithelial infiltrates at the edge with a clear zone from the limbus, epithelial defect smaller than the infiltrate, little AC reaction.
Treat: weak steroid (FML) ± antibiotic for 1–2 weeks. Blepharitis care. Recurrent → oral doxycycline (erythromycin in kids/pregnancy).
Phlyctenulosis: kids/young adults. Photophobia, tearing. White nodule at the limbus with intense local redness. Can march onto the cornea.
Cause: staph (rich countries, rosacea); TB/helminths (developing countries).
Heals in 2–3 weeks → triangular limbal scar. Short topical steroid speeds healing.
chunks.hook: Marginal infiltrate keeps a clear moat from the limbus.

cards.q: Mechanism of marginal keratitis?
cards.a: Hypersensitivity to staphylococcal antigens (immune complex deposition).

cards.q: In developing countries, phlyctenulosis is mostly associated with?

chunks.title: Ocular rosacea
chunks.tldr: Facial flushing, papules, no comedones. Eyes: lid telangiectasia, MGD, chalazia, inferior vessels and thinning. Treat with doxycycline.
points: 6–18% of rosacea patients get eye disease.
Face: telangiectasia, papules, pustules, rhinophyma, flushing.
Lids: margin telangiectasia, posterior blepharitis, recurrent chalazia.
Cornea: inferior PEEs, peripheral vascularisation, marginal keratitis, inferior thinning → can perforate.
Topical: lubricants, lid hygiene, antibiotic to the lid margin, short weak steroid.
Doxycycline 100 mg daily → 50 mg: fixes meibum, anti-inflammatory, anti-collagenase. Erythromycin in kids/pregnancy.
Severe: immunosuppression. Retinoids can help but are banned in pregnancy.
chunks.hook: Red face + red lid margins + thin lower cornea = rosacea.

cards.q: Three mechanisms by which tetracyclines help ocular rosacea?
cards.a: Improve meibum (↓ free fatty acids), anti-inflammatory, anticollagenase.

chunks.title: Mooren ulcer
chunks.tldr: Painful peripheral ulcer with an undermined, overhanging edge, no scleritis, no systemic disease. Treat: steroids → conjunctival resection → systemic immunosuppression.
points: Autoimmune. Exclude infection and systemic disease first.
Type 1: older, one eye, responds well. Type 2: young (Indian subcontinent men), both eyes, aggressive, very painful.
Signs: superficial peripheral ulcer spreading around and then in. Undermined, infiltrated leading edge. Vessels up to the edge.
No scleritis (that's how you tell it from autoimmune PUK).
Complications: astigmatism, perforation after minor trauma, infection.
Treat: hourly topical steroid + antibiotic cover → ciclosporin/tacrolimus → acetylcysteine/doxycycline (anti-collagenase).
Conjunctival resection: 4 mm back from the limbus, 2 mm beyond the ulcer edges.
Systemic immunosuppression early if bilateral/advanced.
chunks.hook: Mooren = Moat with an overhanging bank, and the sclera is calm.

cards.q: Key sign distinguishing Mooren ulcer from PUK with systemic disease?
Typical edge of a Mooren ulcer?

chunks.title: PUK from systemic disease (RA, GPA)
chunks.tldr: Peripheral melt + scleritis → hunt for RA (commonest) or GPA. Can be life-threatening. Needs systemic immunosuppression.
points: Mechanism: immune complexes in peripheral cornea + capillary blockage → collagenases.
Rheumatoid arthritis: commonest. Usually advanced RA, 30% both eyes. Peripheral guttering ('contact lens cornea'), paracentral ulcers.
GPA (Wegener): second commonest. Eye is the first sign in 50%. cANCA.
Others: PAN, relapsing polychondritis, SLE, Crohn.
Treat with rheumatology: systemic steroids, cyclophosphamide, biologics. Local: lubricants, doxycycline, glue/graft.
Other peripheral thinning: dellen (drying next to a bump), furrow degeneration (harmless, elderly), Terrien, pellucid.
chunks.hook: PUK + scleritis = look at the whole patient (it may kill them).

cards.q: Commonest systemic association of PUK?
In which disease is PUK the presenting feature in ~50%?

chunks.title: Terrien marginal degeneration
chunks.tldr: Painless peripheral gutter, usually superior, men (75%), clear zone from the limbus, lipid line at the central edge, epithelium intact. Main problem: astigmatism.
points: Idiopathic thinning. Young adult to elderly, ~75% male, usually both eyes.
Fine yellow-white stromal opacities + superficial vessels, starting superiorly, with a clear zone from the limbus (looks like arcus at first).
Gutter: outer slope gentle, inner slope steep, lipid band at the central edge. No epithelial defect.
Can get pseudopterygia. Perforation rare (trauma).
Treat: safety glasses, contact lenses (scleral, piggyback), crescentic lamellar graft.
Rheumatoid PCUK: punched-out paracentral ulcer in a quiet eye → topical ciclosporin, bandage CL, glue.
chunks.hook: Terrien = Top, Tidy (epithelium intact), lipid Trim.

cards.q: Peripheral superior gutter, intact epithelium, lipid at the central edge, middle-aged man?

chunks.title: Neurotrophic & exposure keratopathy
chunks.tldr: Neurotrophic = numb cornea (CN V) → defect with rolled edges → melt, often painless. Exposure = lids don't close → inferior damage.
points: Neurotrophic causes: trigeminal surgery, stroke, tumour (acoustic neuroma), diabetes, HSV/HZO. Do a full cranial nerve exam.
Stage 1: interpalpebral irregular staining. Stage 2: persistent defect with rolled thickened edges. Stage 3: stromal melt (little pain), infection, perforation.

Treat: stop toxic drops, preservative-free lubricants, anti-collagenase (acetylcysteine, doxycycline), cenegermin (nerve growth factor drops), tape/botox ptosis/tarsorrhaphy, bandage CL, amniotic membrane.
Corneal neurotisation: sural nerve graft from the other side's supratrochlear nerve → sensation back in 6–8 months.
Exposure: lagophthalmos from CN VII palsy, Parkinson, lid scars, post-blepharoplasty, proptosis.
Exposure signs: inferior third PEEs → defect → melt → infection.
Exposure treatment: lubricant/night ointment/tape, bandage or scleral lens, tarsorrhaphy/Frost suture, gold/platinum weight, decompression.
chunks.hook: Numb cornea doesn't complain, so it melts quietly.

cards.q: Topical recombinant nerve growth factor for neurotrophic keratopathy?
Characteristic appearance of a stage 2 neurotrophic defect?
cards.a: Persistent epithelial defect with rolled, thickened edges.

chunks.title: Crystalline keratopathy, Thygeson, filaments
chunks.tldr: Infectious crystalline = branching white crystals in a graft on steroids (Strep viridans). Thygeson = central grey dots in a white eye, loves steroids.
points: Infectious crystalline keratopathy: long-term topical steroid, usually after PK. Grey-white branching stromal crystals, little inflammation, intact epithelium. Strep viridans in a biofilm. Weeks of antibiotics, maybe laser/keratectomy/regraft.
Thygeson SPK: young adults, both eyes, comes and goes for years. Coarse grey raised epithelial dots, mainly central, eye not red.
Thygeson treatment: lubricants → low-dose steroid (very sensitive) → ciclosporin/tacrolimus, soft CL. Antivirals don't help.
Filamentary keratopathy: dry eye, overwearing CL, unstable epithelium (erosions, surgery, drugs), SLK, bullous, neurotrophic, long eye closure.
Filaments: treat the cause, pull them off, acetylcysteine, NSAID drops, hypertonic saline, bandage CL.
chunks.hook: Thygeson: white eye, grey dots.

cards.q: Organism most often in infectious crystalline keratopathy?
Bilateral recurrent central coarse epithelial dots with a white eye?

chunks.title: Recurrent corneal erosion
chunks.tldr: Wakes up with sudden eye pain, often months/years after a scratch (fingernail, paper). Weak epithelial adhesion. Long-term night-time lubricant; refractory → PTK or stromal puncture.
points: Basal epithelium sticks poorly to its basement membrane. Lid rubs it off during sleep.
Causes: old abrasion, corneal dystrophies (esp. EBMD), surgery.
Symptoms: severe pain, photophobia, tears on waking.
Signs: defect may have healed already. Look for loose epithelium, pooling fluorescein, microcysts, map/fingerprint lines. Both eyes → dystrophy. One eye → trauma.
Acute: antibiotic ointment, cycloplegic, no pressure patch, bandage CL if severe, debride loose epithelium, diclofenac, hypertonic saline 5%. Never give anaesthetic drops to take home.
Prevention: lubricant/hypertonic ointment at night for months.
Recurrent: doxycycline + topical steroid (MMP inhibition), long-term bandage CL, debridement + diamond burr or excimer PTK, anterior stromal puncture (off the visual axis).
chunks.hook: Morning ouch after an old scratch = recurrent erosion.

cards.q: Why avoid pressure patching in recurrent erosion?
cards.a: It may impair healing and doesn't improve comfort.

cards.q: Surgical treatment for refractory recurrent erosion?
cards.a: Excimer PTK, diamond burr polishing, or anterior stromal puncture.

chunks.title: Xerophthalmia (vitamin A deficiency)
chunks.tldr: First symptom = night blindness. Bitot spots = foamy patches. Keratomalacia (melt) = medical emergency → high-dose vitamin A.
points: Vitamin A: needed for epithelium, immunity, and photoreceptors.
Causes: malnutrition, malabsorption, alcoholism, faddy diets. Kids worse with measles/diarrhoea.
WHO grades: XN night blindness → X1A conjunctival xerosis → X1B Bitot spots → X2 corneal xerosis → X3 ulcer/keratomalacia (A <⅓, B >⅓) → XS scar → XF fundus.
Bitot spots: triangular foamy keratinised patches in the interpalpebral conjunctiva (Corynebacterium xerosis).
Cornea: dull, PEEs (reversible), keratinisation, keratomalacia (liquefactive melt) → perforation.
Fundus: yellow peripheral dots, low ERG.
Treat: oral vitamin A 200,000 IU (or IM 100,000 IU), diet, lubricants, retinoic acid. Kids can die → emergency.
chunks.hook: Can't see at night → foamy spots → melting cornea.

cards.q: Earliest symptom of vitamin A deficiency?
Foamy triangular patches on the interpalpebral conjunctiva?

chunks.title: Keratoconus: signs
chunks.tldr: Teen/20s, progressive myopia + irregular astigmatism. Signs: oil-drop reflex, scissoring, Vogt striae, Fleischer ring, Munson sign. Topography: inferior steepening.
points: Central/paracentral thinning → cone. Almost always both eyes eventually (one first).
Grade by K: mild <48 D, moderate 48–54, severe >54.
Associations: Down, Ehlers–Danlos, Marfan, OI; VKC/atopy, eye rubbing, LCA, RP, aniridia, blue sclera.
Oil-droplet red reflex. Scissoring on retinoscopy.
Vogt striae: fine vertical deep stromal lines (disappear when you press the globe).
Fleischer ring: iron ring around the base of the cone (see with cobalt blue).
Munson sign: lower lid bulges on downgaze.
Topography: symmetrical bow-tie → asymmetric → inferotemporal steep cone.
Acute hydrops: Descemet tears → sudden stromal oedema, pain. Heals in 6–10 weeks with a scar. Treat: cycloplegic, hypertonic saline, bandage CL, ± intracameral gas.
chunks.hook: KC signs: Oil, Scissors, Vogt, Fleischer, Munson: 'O S V F M — Only Short Vision For Myopes'.

cards.q: Iron ring at the base of a keratoconus cone?
Fine vertical deep stromal lines in keratoconus that disappear on globe pressure?
Sudden corneal oedema in keratoconus from a Descemet break?

chunks.title: Keratoconus: treatment
chunks.tldr: Stop eye rubbing. Glasses → rigid/scleral lenses. Progressing → cross-linking. Advanced → rings or keratoplasty. Never LASIK.
points: No eye rubbing (treat allergy!).
Early: glasses or soft CL. More astigmatism: RGP or scleral lenses.
Corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL): riboflavin + UVA → stiffens the cornea. Used once progression is documented. Can stabilise or reverse slightly.
Intracorneal ring segments: flatten the cone, help CL tolerance.
Keratoplasty: PK or DALK. Past hydrops = contraindication to DALK (Descemet break).
LASIK is contraindicated. Always screen topography before refractive surgery.
chunks.hook: Keratoconus ladder: Specs → RGP → Cross-link → Rings → Graft.

cards.q: Components of corneal collagen cross-linking?
Why is DALK contraindicated after hydrops?
cards.a: There is a break in Descemet membrane.

chunks.title: Pellucid marginal degeneration & keratoglobus
chunks.tldr: Pellucid = thin band inferiorly 4–8 o'clock, 1 mm from the limbus, cornea above it bulges. Topography: 'butterfly' / kissing doves. Keratoglobus = whole cornea thin and globular, ruptures easily.
points: Pellucid: adults, both eyes. Crescent 1–2 mm wide, inferior, 1 mm from the limbus. Epithelium intact.
No Fleischer ring, no Vogt striae, hydrops rare (unlike KC).
Topography: butterfly pattern, severe against-the-rule astigmatism, inferior steepening.
Treat: glasses, CL; cross-linking promising; various grafts/resections.
Keratoglobus: congenital (differential: congenital glaucoma, megalocornea) or acquired. Globular bulge, diffuse thinning.
Keratoglobus ruptures with minor trauma → protective glasses.
chunks.hook: Pellucid: the bulge sits above the thin band ('beer belly over the belt').

cards.q: Location of thinning in pellucid marginal degeneration?
cards.a: Inferior band, 4–8 o'clock, about 1 mm from the limbus.

cards.q: Topography pattern of pellucid?

chunks.title: Epithelial & Bowman dystrophies
chunks.tldr: EBMD (Cogan, map-dot-fingerprint) → recurrent erosions. Meesmann → tiny epithelial cysts. Reis–Bücklers / Thiel–Behnke (TGFBI) → erosions in childhood.
points: Dystrophies: usually both eyes, one layer, slow, genetic.
EBMD (Cogan / map-dot-fingerprint): mostly sporadic (degeneration). Maps, dots (microcysts), fingerprint lines, blebs. See best on retroillumination. ~10% get erosions in their 30s.
Bilateral erosions without trauma → think EBMD.
Meesmann: AD, keratin genes. Myriad tiny uniform intraepithelial cysts. Mild.
Others: Lisch, gelatinous drop-like, subepithelial mucinous.
Reis–Bücklers (CBD1, GCD3): AD, TGFBI. Bowman replaced by scar. Grey geographic opacities, severe childhood erosions, reduced sensation. PTK helps.
Thiel–Behnke (CBD2): honeycomb pattern, milder. 'Curly fibres' on EM.
chunks.hook: Map, Dot, Fingerprint = the epithelium's messy basement.

cards.q: Other name for Cogan epithelial basement membrane dystrophy?
Honeycomb subepithelial opacities with childhood erosions?

chunks.title: Lattice dystrophy (amyloid)
chunks.tldr: Lattice = Amyloid: Congo red, apple-green birefringence. TGFBI type: branching lines, erosions ~age 10. Gelsolin type (Meretoja) = systemic neuropathy.
points: Lattice TGFBI type (LCD1): AD. Refractile dots → fine branching lattice lines, periphery spared → central haze. Erosions end of the first decade. Reduced sensation.
Often needs keratoplasty; recurs in the graft.
Lattice gelsolin type (LCD2, Meretoja): AD, GSN gene. Sparse lines spreading from the periphery inward. Cranial/peripheral neuropathy, mask-like face, autonomic problems.
Histology: amyloid → Congo red, green birefringence under polarised light.
chunks.hook: Lattice = Lines of amyLoid.

cards.q: Stain for lattice dystrophy deposits?
Lattice dystrophy with facial palsy and neuropathy?

chunks.title: Granular, macular, Schnyder (the stromal 3)
chunks.tldr: Classic trio: Marilyn Monroe Always Gets Her Men in LA City → Macular = Mucopolysaccharide (Alcian blue). Granular = Hyaline (Masson). Lattice = Amyloid (Congo red).
points: Granular type 1: AD, TGFBI. Sharp white 'breadcrumb/sugar' deposits with clear stroma between, spares the limbus. Glare. Hyaline → Masson trichrome red. Graft by ~50s.
Granular type 2 (Avellino): hyaline + amyloid. Stellate/ring lesions. Trauma and refractive surgery make it worse.

Macular dystrophy: AR (the odd one out!), CHST6, common in Iceland. Ill-defined grey spots, no clear stroma between, reaches the limbus, thin cornea. Early vision loss, lots of erosions. GAGs → Alcian blue / colloidal iron. Needs PK, recurs.
Schnyder: AD, UBIAD1. Lipid/cholesterol. Central haze, crystals in only ~50%, prominent arcus. Check lipids.
François central cloudy: grey polygonal posterior opacities, harmless (≈ posterior crocodile shagreen).
chunks.hook: Marilyn Monroe Always Gets Her Men in LA City.

cards.q: Which stromal dystrophy is autosomal recessive?
Deposit and stain in granular dystrophy?
Which dystrophy is worsened by LASIK/trauma?

chunks.title: Fuchs endothelial dystrophy
chunks.tldr: Middle-aged woman, guttata ('beaten metal') → oedema, blur worse in the morning → bullae. Fix = DSAEK/DMEK. Risky cataract surgery if CCT >640 µm.
points: Accelerated endothelial loss, both eyes. More in women, slight link with open-angle glaucoma. Genes: TCF4 (most), COL8A2 (early onset).
Cornea guttata: warts on Descemet. Specular reflection: dark spots → 'beaten metal'.
Stromal oedema → blur worst in the morning (eyes closed overnight), better later in the day.
Epithelial oedema → microcysts → bullae → rupture = very painful.
Conservative: hypertonic saline 5%, lower IOP, hair dryer at arm's length. Ruptured bullae: bandage CL, cycloplegic, antibiotic.
Surgery: DSAEK / DMEK (posterior lamellar) or PK. Poor vision: conjunctival flap, amniotic membrane.
New: Rho-kinase inhibitor drops.
Cataract surgery can tip them into oedema: protect the endothelium. Consider a triple procedure. Oedema unlikely if CCT <630–640 µm.
chunks.hook: Fuchs = Foggy in the morning.

cards.q: Why is vision worse in the morning in Fuchs dystrophy?
cards.a: Overnight lid closure reduces tear evaporation, so corneal oedema accumulates.

cards.q: Preferred surgery for Fuchs with clear stroma?

chunks.title: PPCD & CHED
chunks.tldr: PPCD = vesicles/bands on the endothelium, usually no symptoms, link with Alport. CHED = cloudy thick corneas in a baby (CHED2 AR, ± deafness = Harboyan).
points: Posterior polymorphous dystrophy: AD. Endothelial cells act like epithelium. Vesicles, bands, diffuse lesions. Usually found by chance. Associations: iris anomalies, glaucoma, Alport syndrome.
CHED: Descemet thickened, endothelium degenerates.
CHED2: AR, SLC4A11, cloudy at birth, nystagmus, no tearing. ± deafness (Harboyan).
CHED1: AD, starts in year 1–2, photophobia + watering.
Vision often better than it looks. Treat with keratoplasty.
chunks.hook: Cloudy newborn cornea: think STUMPED (Sclerocornea, Tears in Descemet, Ulcer, Metabolic, Peters, Endothelial dystrophy (CHED), Dermoid).

cards.q: Posterior polymorphous dystrophy is associated with which syndrome?
Congenital corneal clouding + deafness?

chunks.title: Age-related corneal changes
chunks.tldr: Arcus = lipid ring with a clear gap to the limbus (young → check lipids). Others are harmless: Vogt girdle, farinata, crocodile shagreen.
points: Arcus senilis: lipid, starts top and bottom → full ring ~1 mm. Sharp outer edge with a clear zone. Under ~50 (arcus juvenilis) → dyslipidaemia.
Vogt limbal girdle: chalky white crescents at 3 and 9 o'clock. Type I = 'Swiss cheese' holes + clear zone (like band keratopathy). Type II = no holes. Harmless.
Cornea farinata: tiny flour-like deep stromal dots. Harmless.
Crocodile shagreen: grey polygonal opacities with clear cracks between (anterior or posterior). Harmless.
West Indian punctate keratopathy: 1–4 tiny white dots with a halo at Bowman level, elderly West Indian men. Harmless.
chunks.hook: Young arcus = check cholesterol. Old arcus = birthday candles.

cards.q: Arcus in a 30-year-old suggests?
White chalky limbal crescents at 3 and 9 o'clock?

chunks.title: Band keratopathy & lipid keratopathy
chunks.tldr: Band keratopathy = calcium in Bowman, interpalpebral, Swiss-cheese holes. Kids → JIA uveitis. Treat with EDTA chelation.
points: Causes, ocular: chronic uveitis (esp. JIA), glaucoma, phthisis, silicone oil in AC, chronic oedema/keratitis.
Causes, metabolic (high calcium): hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, milk-alkali, sarcoid, renal failure, Paget, myeloma. Also gout, ichthyosis, age.
Signs: starts at the edges of the interpalpebral zone with a clear zone at the limbus → spreads centrally, chalky plaque with small holes.
Treat: scrape epithelium + calcium, rub with EDTA 1.5–3% for 15–20 min. Or diamond burr, PTK.
Lipid keratopathy: primary (rare, no vessels) or secondary (much commoner) leaking from vessels after HSV/HZO.
Lipid treatment: control inflammation, laser/needle cautery of feeder vessels, graft.
chunks.hook: Band = Bowman + calcium Bricks. EDTA = Eats Da Tough A(calcium).

cards.q: Chelating agent used for band keratopathy?
Child with band keratopathy: likely ocular cause?
cards.a: Chronic anterior uveitis from juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

chunks.title: Spheroidal, Salzmann, AWE
chunks.tldr: Spheroidal = amber droplets in outdoor workers (UV). Salzmann = blue-grey nodules on chronically irritated corneas, peel them off.
points: Spheroidal degeneration (Labrador / climatic droplet keratopathy): men working outdoors, UV. Amber granules in the interpalpebral superficial stroma → coalesce → raised. Sunglasses; keratectomy if needed.
Salzmann nodular degeneration: hyaline nodules in front of Bowman. After trachoma, dry eye, blepharitis, allergy. White/blue-grey raised nodules ± iron line.
Salzmann treatment: lubricate, peel off (superficial keratectomy) + diamond burr ± MMC, PTK.

Advancing wave-like epitheliopathy: irregular epithelial plaque creeping in from the superior limbus. CL wear, CL solutions, glaucoma drops, surgery, rosacea. Treat cause, silver nitrate 1% to the limbus or cryo.
chunks.hook: Spheroidal = Sun (amber droplets). Salzmann = Scabs on irritated corneas.

cards.q: Amber superficial stromal granules in a fisherman?

chunks.title: Metabolic cornea clues
chunks.tldr: Crystals = cystinosis. Copper ring = Wilson (Kayser–Fleischer). Vortex = Fabry (or amiodarone). Cloudy = MPS (not Hunter/Sanfilippo).
points: Cystinosis: AR, CTNS. Cystine crystals in cornea and conjunctiva → photophobia, erosions. Kidney failure in kids. Cysteamine drops dissolve crystals.
Mucopolysaccharidoses: mostly AR. Coarse face, skeleton, heart, learning problems. Corneal clouding in all except Hunter and Sanfilippo. Also RP-like retinopathy, optic atrophy.

Wilson disease: low caeruloplasmin, copper everywhere. Kayser–Fleischer ring = brown-gold copper in peripheral Descemet (top and bottom first; gonioscopy for subtle ones). 95% of those with neuro signs. Sunflower cataract. Fades with penicillamine.
LCAT deficiency: grey dots in the stroma, arcus-like. Norum (systemic, kidneys) / fish eye disease (cornea only).
Immunoprotein deposits: myeloma, Waldenström, MGUS → flake-like posterior stromal opacities. May be the first sign.
Tyrosinaemia type 2: AR. Pseudodendrites in kids + painful hand/foot calluses.

Fabry disease: X-linked, α-galactosidase A. Vortex keratopathy (75%, first sign), spoke-like posterior cataract, corkscrew conjunctival vessels. Burning limb pain, angiokeratomas, kidney and heart disease.
chunks.hook: Fabry = Fan-shaped vortex. Wilson = copper Wedding ring on Descemet.

cards.q: Where is copper deposited in a Kayser–Fleischer ring?
Which two MPS types lack corneal clouding?
Vortex keratopathy + burning limb pain + angiokeratomas?

chunks.title: Contact lens uses & problems
chunks.tldr: Therapeutic CLs: vision (KC), healing, pain relief (bullous), sealing. Problems: hypoxia (microcysts, vessels), sterile infiltrates, toxic, and infection (biggest risk).
points: Optical: irregular astigmatism (KC, post-graft), surface irregularity, anisometropia.
Healing: persistent defects, recurrent erosions.
Pain: bullous keratopathy, filaments, Thygeson, trichiasis.
Integrity: cap a descemetocoele, splint small wounds, cover glue.
Other: ptosis props, keep the fornices open, drug delivery.

Hypoxia: SPK (3 and 9 o'clock in rigid lenses = incomplete blink), tight lens syndrome (ring of conjunctival indentation), acute microcysts and painful erosions after overwear, chronic vessels (<1.5 mm is common). Fix: silicone hydrogel/RGP, looser fit, less wear.
Hypersensitivity: sterile marginal infiltrates, little/no defect. Stop lenses (treat as infection if unsure).
Toxic: hydrogen peroxide not neutralised (acute), preservatives like thiomersal/BAK (chronic) → switch to dailies.
Infection: CL = biggest risk factor for bacterial keratitis (RGP lowest). Tap water → Acanthamoeba.
chunks.hook: CL trouble = Hungry for oxygen, Hypersensitive, Hurt by chemicals, or Harbouring bugs.

cards.q: 3 and 9 o'clock staining in a rigid lens wearer?
Ring of conjunctival indentation and staining around the cornea in a CL wearer?

chunks.title: Small eyes & big corneas
chunks.tldr: Microcornea <10 mm (after age 2). Nanophthalmos = axial length <20 mm → angle closure, and surgery causes effusions ('small eye, big trouble'). Megalocornea ≥13 mm, X-linked, males.
points: Normal corneal diameter: 10 mm at birth → 12 mm by age 2.
Microcornea: ≤10 mm (<9 mm newborn), steep, hyperopic, shallow AC. Linked with glaucoma, cataract, PFV, coloboma.
Microphthalmos: whole eye small (≥2 SD below). Simple (nanophthalmos) or complex (coloboma, orbital cyst). ~50% have systemic problems. Fetal alcohol, infections.
Nanophthalmos: AL <20 mm, both eyes, high hyperopia, angle closure (big lens, small eye). Surgery → aqueous misdirection, choroidal effusion.
Anophthalmos: no visible globe (± cyst).
Megalocornea: ≥13 mm, X-linked (90% male), very deep AC, myopia/astigmatism, lens subluxation, pigment dispersion. Not progressive. (Differential: buphthalmos, which has high IOP and Haab striae.)

Sclerocornea: no clear limbus, white periphery. Cornea plana: flat → high hyperopia. Keratectasia: bulging opaque cornea (intrauterine perforation). Posterior keratoconus: back surface dip, vision OK.
chunks.hook: Small eye, big trouble (nanophthalmos surgery).
